Series::standardize¶

Back to SeriesStatAccessor API Reference

Signature¶

Series::standardize() const -> Series
Series::standardize(std::int64_t dim) const -> Series
Series::stat.standardize(...) -> Series
Series::stat().standardize(...) -> Series

What It Does¶

standardize() centers the data and divides by its spread while preserving the original shape.

This is the higher-level normalization counterpart to center:

  • center() removes only location

  • standardize() removes location and rescales dispersion

In other words, standardization asks for more than “shift the values around zero.” It asks for “shift them around zero and put them on a comparable spread.”

That makes standardize() a stronger next step than center():

  • center() tells you deviations from the mean

  • standardize() tells you deviations from the mean in spread-scaled units

Overload Map¶

standardize()

Apply one global mean and one global spread to the entire Series.

standardize(dim)

Apply one mean and one spread per lane along the chosen axis, then broadcast that normalization back across the original shape.

stat.standardize(...) / stat().standardize(...)

Equivalent accessor spellings.

There is no keepdim flag because the transform preserves shape.

Parameters¶

dim (std::int64_t)

The axis whose lanes should be normalized independently.

Important details:

  • dim = 0 standardizes column-wise on a 2D Series

  • dim = 1 standardizes row-wise on a 2D Series

  • negative dims count from the back, so -1 means the last axis

  • each lane gets its own mean and its own spread

Returns¶

Series A new Series with the same shape as the input, but centered and rescaled along the chosen scope.

Gradient¶

This is a floating normalization transform intended to participate in ordinary numeric pipelines.

Examples¶

The examples below are arranged to teach the two big choices:

  • global versus lane-wise normalization

  • which lane direction dim is actually selecting

Unless stated otherwise, they use:

auto values = pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}, {2, 3});

Example 1. Global standardization uses one mean and one spread for the entire series.

std::cout << values.standardize();

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=[[-1.4638501, -0.87831007, -0.29277002],
  [0.29277002, 0.87831007, 1.4638501]]

Everything is measured relative to one global center and one global spread, so the two rows do not end up looking identical.

Example 2. Row-wise standardization normalizes each row independently.

std::cout << values.stat.standardize(1);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=[[-1.2247449, 0, 1.2247449],
  [-1.2247449, 0, 1.2247449]]

Each row is normalized by its own mean and spread, so the rows now share the same normalized shape. The direct values.standardize(1) spelling follows the same semantics; this example uses the verified accessor call.

Example 3. The accessor spelling stat().standardize(dim) reaches the same transformation.

std::cout << values.stat().standardize(1);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=[[-1.2247449, 0, 1.2247449],
  [-1.2247449, 0, 1.2247449]]

This is the same result as Example 2. The accessor is organizational, not a different algorithm.

Example 4. Column-wise standardization gives a different answer because the lanes changed.

std::cout << values.standardize(0);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=[[-1, -1, -1],
  [1, 1, 1]]

Each column has only two values here, so each column becomes a simple [-1, 1] pattern after standardization.

Example 5. Negative dimensions count from the back, so -1 means the last axis.

std::cout << values.standardize(-1);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=[[-1.2247449, 0, 1.2247449],
  [-1.2247449, 0, 1.2247449]]

On this shape, the last axis is the row axis, so the result matches Example 2.

Example 6. Constant lanes are handled stably rather than exploding.

auto constant_rows = pluss::make_series({2, 2, 2, 5, 5, 5}, {2, 3});
std::cout << constant_rows.standardize(1);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=[[0, 0, 0],
  [0, 0, 0]]

This is an important verified behavior:

  • constant lanes do not turn into NaNs

  • they collapse cleanly to zeros

Reading The Numbers¶

Look again at the row-wise output from Example 2:

data=[[-1.2247449, 0, 1.2247449],
  [-1.2247449, 0, 1.2247449]]

For the row [1, 2, 3], that magnitude corresponds to dividing by sqrt(2/3), not by sample standard deviation 1.

That matters if you are checking results by hand: the current verified behavior is population-style normalization on this surface.

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • standardize() preserves shape. If you expected fewer dimensions, you wanted a reduction, not a transform.

  • Choosing the wrong dim changes the meaning substantially. Row-wise and column-wise standardization are often both “reasonable” but answer different questions.

  • Constant lanes normalize to zero rather than failing or producing NaNs. This is convenient, but it also means “all zeros” can mean “no spread was present.”

  • A dim outside the valid axis range fails.

  • The current verified behavior is population-style normalization.

Summary¶

Use standardize() when both offset and spread should be removed while shape is preserved:

  • standardize() uses one global mean and spread

  • standardize(dim) uses one mean and spread per lane

  • constant lanes collapse to zero on the current public surface

See Also¶

  • Series::center: mean removal without scale normalization.

  • Series::std: report the spread instead of applying it.
